12 Methods and tools to improve quantum software quality: a survey

Mahsa Radnejad
Khushdeep Kaur
Houbing Song
Lei Zhang

Note: The first two coauthors have made equal contributions to this chapter.

Abstract

With recent breakthroughs in quantum computing, it has become a coming reality instead of a promising future. Quantum computing applications offer revolutionary potential across multiple domains including artificial intelligence (AI), optimization, healthcare, energy, and space, known as quantum advantage.

The power of quantum computing relies on novel quantum algorithms, quantum software, and hardware. Unlike classical software, quantum software has unique features because of quantum mechanics such as superposition and noncloning. This opens a new research field – quantum software engineering (QSE). While the software engineering (SE) research community became aware of this need in 2019, we noticed the lack of a comprehensive investigation of state-of-the-art technologies and tools to improve quantum software quality. Testing and debugging are the two most efficient approaches to assure software quality in classical SE. In QSE, testing and debugging quantum programs become challenging due to quantum mechanics. While we can leverage some best practices from the classical world, new techniques and tools are needed to address the concerns in QSE.

In this chapter, we first conduct a survey study of the state-of-the-art technologies and tools for testing and debugging quantum software. This study includes but is not limited to quantum bug pattern analysis and detection, quantum software testing techniques and classification, and quantum debugging techniques. In the second place, we provide our visions and insights of testing and debugging quantum software in terms of challenges and opportunities for improving quantum software quality. This survey has the potential to foster a research community committed to developing novel methods and tools for QSE.

Keywords: Quantum computing, quantum software engineering, quantum software testing, quantum software debugging,

12.1 Introduction

Quantum computing utilizes quantum mechanisms to process quantum information, which can be exponentially faster than what is possible with classical computers (CCs). The supremacy of quantum computers (QCs) over CCs is called “quantum advantage.” The potential of quantum computing is grounded in the properties of quantum physics including but not limited to superposition, wavefunction collapse, entanglement, and no-cloning [1].

In 1981, Dr. Richard Feyman discussed using a QC to simulate quantum systems [2]. In 1985, Deutsch’s Quantum Turing Machine, which formalizes the concept of using QCs to perform quantum computations, was introduced by Dr. David Deutsch [3]. However, it was not until 1998 that the first QC was created by the Los Alamos National Laboratory, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and the University of California at Berkeley with only two qubits (quantum bits [4]). In the last decade, quantum hardware has grown dramatically – the current qubit record holder is IBM’s Osprey computer, with 433 qubits (but IBM has not yet released details about how it performs until this chapter is completed).

Like CCs, QCs have both hardware and software. Meanwhile, the hardware of QCs is being developed rapidly. On the software side, quantum programs are mostly on the lower lever, that is, we use assembly programming languages to manipulate qubits. Existing quantum software development platforms and programming languages include but are not limited to IBM Qiskit (based on OpenQASM [5]), Microsoft Quantum Development Kit (Q#, [6]), Tensorflow Quantum [7], Cirq [8], Scaffold [9], and Silq (considered to be a high-level programming language for quantum computing [10]). The development of quantum software is harnessed by software engineering (SE) principles. Quantum software engineering (QSE) plays a significant role in developing quantum software systems [11]. QSE covers the whole quantum software development life cycle including requirements engineering, system modeling, implementation, testing, maintenance, and evolution.

While most quantum programming languages are at lower levels, QSE methods and tools are similar to what happened in the classical world back in the 1960s and 1970s. At that time, the waterfall model was just introduced. However, the field lacked efficient methods and tools to maintain the quality of the software and the speed of software development. The history is repeating itself in QSE. Due to quantum mechanics, it is extremely challenging to test and debug quantum programs. For example, the indeterminacy of quantum computing produces random results. Thus, testing a quantum program also generates indeterminate test results, which may pass or fail randomly. This leads to flaky tests, which should be avoided during software development [12].

The increasing size and complexity of quantum programs have led to a rise in bugs within quantum source code, paralleling similar challenges in classical software development. While classical SE has a rich array of tools and methodologies for bug detection and elimination [13, 14], quantum software development demands novel approaches to enhance quality. Existing research explores adapting classical practices to quantum such as search-based testing techniques [15, 16, 17]. Notable contributions include QBugs [18], which introduces reproducible bugs in quantum algorithms, fostering controlled quantum software testing and debugging experiments. Tailored approaches have emerged, encompassing fuzz testing [19, 20, 21] and mutation testing [22, 23, 24]. Novel tools like QuanFuzz [20], QMutPy [23], and Muskit [24] have been proposed. Researchers delve into bug pattern identification [25], comprehensive bug fix studies [26], and static analysis [27]. Additionally, classical debugging elements like assertions have been adapted to the quantum landscape, with runtime, statistical, and dynamic assertions applied to quantum circuits [28, 29, 30, 31]. The evolving field reflects a concerted effort to develop specialized methodologies, tools, and techniques for testing and debugging quantum software, ensuring the reliability and efficiency of quantum computing technology.

We have two contributions in this chapter. First, we present a comprehensive survey of testing and debugging techniques in QSE. We summarize existing methods and tools for quantum bug pattern detection, bug-fix pattern detection, bug benchmarking, testing, and debugging. We categorize bug pattern detection and testing techniques.

Second, we also provide thorough insights about how to improve the quality of quantum software, that is, the challenges, research directions, and opportunities. We hope this survey will help both researchers and practitioners prepare the knowledge foundations of QSE and foster novel research ideas in QSE.

The chapter is structured as follows. Section 12.2 introduces the bug patterns, bug pattern detection techniques, and benchmarks in QSE. Section 12.3 describes testing methods, tools, and classification for quantum programs. In Section 12.4, we review debugging tactics and put them into three categories. In Section 12.5, we discuss research challenges and opportunities for quantum software testing and debugging. Then, we conclude the chapter in Section12.6.

12.2 Quantum bugs

In this section, we will introduce quantum software bug patterns, bug pattern detection tools, and quantum bug benchmarks, respectively.

12.2.1 Bug patterns

A software bug is formally defined as an aberrant behavior within a program characterized by an error, flaw, or fault in the design, development, or operation of the software, causing it to deviate from its originally intended functionality [32]. To address this issue, various SE activities, including program analysis, debugging, and software testing, can be performed, focusing on developing techniques and tools for detecting and resolving errors.

Software bugs are from various sources. Syntax bugs are associated with incorrect characters in source code, and semantic bugs occur when there are no compiling errors, but the program does not perform the correct logic. A comprehensive understanding of the behaviors associated with quantum program bugs is imperative in debugging and testing quantum software. On the other hand, just as bugs exist in classical testing and detection programs, they are equally prevalent within quantum programs. The significance of this issue is poised to increase with the progression of quantum programming languages, such as Q# and Cirq, all of which play a pivotal role in shaping the quantum software landscape.

In recent years, investigations into bugs and debugging in quantum software have contributed to heightened awareness among researchers regarding the existence of bugs and the need for their subsequent mitigation in quantum programming.

Huang and Martonosi [28, 33] propose a range of bugs and checked defenses against these bugs in quantum programs. They recognized this as a critical issue against the increasing progress of quantum computing. Their study focuses on the types of bugs in specific quantum programs to support the debugging of quantum software. According to the experience gained, they created a classification of bugs in quantum computing.

Zhao et al. [25] present some bug patterns in the Qiskit framework, along with their classification. They offer a comprehensive exploration of QSE in general, highlighting various tools, approaches, and unresolved issues in the field.

Paltenghi and Pradel [34] focus on the bugs on quantum computing platforms and present an empirical study of real-world bugs in open-source quantum programs. Their research encompasses an exhaustive statistical analysis of bugs and introduces several pertinent bug patterns within quantum computing platforms.

Luo et al. [26] extend some new bugs to improve the procedures based on classification used in the work of Paltenghi and Pradel [34] in quantum programs. They gathered 223 real-world bug cases and their solutions from various quantum programming languages and development platforms such as Qiskit, Q#, and Cirq. These bugs were categorized into four primary groups: application programming interface (API)-related, incorrect application logic, math-related, and others, each with its subcategories. This categorization offers a detailed understanding of quantum program bugs, aiding in the testing and debugging of such programs. Their study is noted as a pioneering effort in addressing bugs in quantum software.

Table 12.1 presents a comprehensive list of bug patterns in quantum programs, detailing each section with cause/descriptions, categories, bug patterns, and references. This compilation was inspired by Zhao et al. [25], who provided a list of bug patterns; we expanded upon this by incorporating additional patterns from recent articles and research [26, 34, 35]. The table delineates five main categories, that is, (1) initialization, (2) gate operation, (3) measurement, (4) logic, and (5) API. Note that the list of quantum bug categories in Table 12.1 is not exhaustive, but a highlight of common quantum bug patterns.

Table 12.1:Quantum bug patterns.

Category

Bug pattern

Cause/description

Initialization

Unequal classical bits and qubits

Classical bits are smaller in magnitude than qubits used for operations or measurements [25].

Insufficient initial qubits

A quantum circuit should be initialized with enough qubits; otherwise, it may cause errors in the quantum circuit [25].

Inappropriate modification of register size

Changing the register size can modify its hash value and bits, making it unsuitable as a key in structures like sets [25].

Gate operation

Custom gates are not recognized

Custom gates may violate the nature of quantum mechanics [25].

Measurement

Over repeated measurement

Iterations of measurements can exceed the capacity and cause unintended consequences [25].

Incorrect operations after measurement

Continual changes to measured qubits including state changes and reentanglement with other qubits [25].

Method measure_all

Developers may not know that measure_all autogenerates classical registers for storing all measured qubits [25].

Logic

Incorrect application logic

Errors in the application’s logic are often unique to quantum computing platforms (subcategories can also be found in [26, 34]).

API

Misuse of methods or formula

Errors from improper method usage like incorrect arguments, misspelled names, or wrong mathematical models in code [26, 34].

First, initialization in quantum computing is a critical phase where classical bits and qubits are prepared for subsequent operations. The bug patterns in this category highlight issues such as (1) unequal magnitudes between classical bits and qubits during initialization [25], (2) the potential inadequacy of initial qubits in specific methods [25], and (3) the risks associated with inappropriate modifications to register size [25]. These patterns underscore the importance of precision and consistency in setting up the foundational elements of quantum programs. “Unequal classical bits and qubits” is a bug pattern in this category that occurs when the number of classical bits is less than the number of qubits, which complicates the storage of measurement results. Moreover, “insufficient initial qubits” occur in certain parametric circuits like the TwoLocal method, where there are not enough qubits for the needs of the circuit. In addition, the bug pattern “inappropriate modification of register size” in quantum programming occurs when changing a register’s size leads to errors, especially in complex circuits, by altering the hash values of the register and its bits, thus affecting its usage in data structures like sets.

Second, in quantum computing, the effective operation of custom gates is paramount for the accuracy of quantum programs. The bug pattern “custom gates are not recognized” highlights challenges arising when attempting to create controlling gates larger than three qubits, violating the principle of two-qubit entanglement [25]. Recognizing custom gates is crucial for the proper execution of quantum algorithms, and deviations from entanglement principles can lead to recognition issues, impacting the reliability of quantum computations. Addressing this bug pattern is essential for ensuring the precise functioning of quantum circuits and maintaining the integrity of quantum algorithms.

Third, measurement serves as a pivotal process, extracting crucial information from quantum systems. The bug pattern “over repeated measurement” [25] highlights the significance of judiciously managing the quantity of measurement iterations to prevent unintended consequences, emphasizing the delicate balance needed in this critical phase. “Incorrect operations after measurement” [25] delves into the nuanced complexities of postmeasurement modifications to qubits, encompassing state alterations and re-entanglement, shedding light on the potential challenges in maintaining the integrity of quantum states. The introduction of the method measure_all adds an extra layer of insight, revealing its automatic generation of a classical register to store all measured qubits [25], providing developers with a valuable awareness of the automatic processes that might influence their quantum programs.

Fourth, the correct application logic is paramount for the success of any computing paradigm, and quantum computing is no exception. This category focuses on bug patterns stemming from mistakes within the application’s logic [26, 34]. Unlike issues encountered in classical computing, the identified bugs in this category are distinctly tailored to the intricacies of quantum computing platforms. This distinctiveness arises from the unique principles of quantum mechanics and the specialized requirements of quantum algorithms. Identifying and addressing these logic-related issues becomes imperative for developers aspiring to craft resilient and error-free quantum programs.

Last but not least, API interactions play a vital role in facilitating the effective utilization of quantum resources. Bug patterns in this category are associated with the misuse of methods or formulas, representing instances where developers may inadvertently deviate from the intended use of specific functions. The bug pattern “misuse of methods or formula” sheds light on errors such as employing an incorrect number of arguments, misspelling method names, or applying inaccurate mathematical formulas or models in the quantum code [26, 34]. The API category serves as a guide for developers to navigate these potential pitfalls, ensuring the proper integration of quantum methods and formulas to enable the seamless execution of quantum algorithms.

12.2.2 Bug pattern detection techniques

Bug pattern detection, in the realm of software development, entails the systematic procedure of recognizing and categorizing errors or flaws automatically within software programs. In the context of quantum programming, the focal objective of bug pattern detection is to discern and resolve programming challenges distinct from quantum computing.

The research of quantum software bug pattern detection is critical because analyzing quantum bug patterns helps developers understand the uniqueness of quantum bugs and develop tools for fix prediction. In the last few years, there have been several research studies about static bug detectors in quantum programs. QChecker [27] is a specialized static analysis tool meticulously crafted for quantum programs developed in Qiskit. It encompasses modules that extract program data through abstract syntax trees (ASTs) and identify bugs by applying pattern-based detection methods.

LintQ [36] is a static analysis framework designed to detect bugs and patterns in quantum programs by using abstractions that reason about common concepts in quantum computing without relying on the details of the underlying quantum computing platform. The authors evaluate the performance of LintQ and show that it has a precision of 80.5% when detecting quantum software errors. Our previous study pushes the research of bug pattern detection even further by proposing an automated bug-fix pattern detection tool [37]. We leverage ASTs and regular expressions to check the syntax and semantics of bug-fix pairs and detect patterns in terms of initialization, operations, and measurements.

12.2.3 Quantum bug benchmark

Quantum bug benchmarks can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of bug pattern detection techniques and debugging approaches. Benchmarks can also provide quantitative comparisons among different bug detection and debugging techniques.

Campos and Souto [18] introduce a benchmark named QBugs for quantum software systems such as ProjectQ and Qiskit. QBugs provides a collection of reproducible bugs, and it introduces essential concepts for establishing a benchmark, serving as a foundational component for building an experimental framework. This framework aids in evaluating and comparing new research efforts while ensuring the reproducibility of prior research outcomes in the realm of QSE. Moreover, the work also addresses the challenges and potential future directions related to the development of QBugs.

Zhao et al. [35] introduce Bugs4Q, a novel benchmark comprising 36 real-world bugs extracted from four IBM Qiskit programs (i.e., Terra, Aer, Ignis, and Aqua). The main purpose of Bugs4Q is to facilitate quantum software testing and debugging of quantum software by providing real-world test cases to identify and address buggy behaviors. It aggregates and categorizes reproducible Qiskit program bugs, making them publicly available for research purposes. Moreover, Zhao et al. [38] expanded on their work by enhancing Bugs4Q, which now encompasses 42 manually validated real bugs from Qiskit programming, along with corresponding test cases to replicate the faulty behaviors. This suite serves as a user-friendly platform for executing Qiskit programs and grants access to both the buggy and stable versions, enabling reproducible research and benchmarking of Qiskit debugging and testing tools.

12.3 Quantum software testing

The need for quantum software testing has garnered considerable attention, especially since the first publication of QSE at the international conference on SE in 2019 [2]. Quantum software testing focuses on detecting faults in quantum programs and cost-effectively identifying quantum errors [39]. Quantum programmers may encounter challenges when testing quantum software due to quantum mechanics such as superposition, entanglement, and no-cloning. For example, a single testing run cannot describe the whole probability distribution because of the random nature of quantum computing [29]. However, there exist similarities between QSE and classical SE (especially classical software that produces probability distributions). Miranskyy and Zhang [2] discuss the possibilities to leverage some classical SE best practices to quantum software development, focusing on testing activities, such as white box and black box testing.

In this section, we will explore the advancements in quantum software testing methods, across four categories, that is, white box testing, black box testing, dynamic testing, and static testing.

  • White box testing: White box testing is a method to test the application at the source code level. It offers the advantage of enabling a more profound analysis of the predicates delineating each model operation, thereby potentially enabling the generation of tests of greater sophistication. As discussed by Miranskyy et al. [40], white box testing techniques are not limited to traditional software but can also be effectively employed in QC simulators. This approach involves a meticulous examination of the internal code listings, enabling the execution of standard white box activities, such as code reviews and inspections, even within the context of quantum computing.

  • Black box testing: Black box testing is a method of testing approach applicable across all levels of testing and entails the evaluation of software functionality without delving into its internal composition or mechanisms. Testers utilizing this method concentrate exclusively on the software’s input and output behavior, devoid of knowledge regarding its underlying implementation, aiming to ascertain its adherence to specified requirements and expected performance. Black box testing in the context of quantum computing refers to the testing approach where the internal workings of a quantum program running on an actual QC cannot be observed directly, and the program is treated as a black box. This is in contrast to white box testing, which can be performed on QC simulators where the internal code listing can be examined [40].

  • Dynamic testing: Dynamic testing is a fundamental approach within software testing, characterized by the live execution of software code to assess its real-time behavior and performance. This methodology offers several advantages, such as its proficiency in revealing elusive errors and defects, contributing significantly to overall testing quality.

  • Moreover, dynamic testing, by subjecting the software to execution in a true-to-life operational context, provides an authentic evaluation of its performance and functionality, delivering valuable insights into real-world operation. However, due to the nature of real-time execution, dynamic testing can be time-intensive for QSE, particularly when dealing with a multitude of test cases, which is common in quantum programs because of probability distributions in quantum mechanics.

  • Static testing: Static testing, a well-established discipline in SE, involves the meticulous analysis of source code to preemptively identify potential defects, all without the need for code execution. Employing specialized code analysis tools, static testing inspects the codebase, flagging potential issues for further investigation and resolution. A key advantage is its capacity to operate before the existence of an executable software version, efficiently detecting insidious faults like memory leaks. This approach also excels in fault localization, as it tends to expose symptoms near their root causes. Utilizing compilers or parsers aligned with the project’s programming language, static testing systematically constructs a comprehensive representation of the codebase, facilitating the identification of potential issues and enhancing software quality and reliability.

  • Numerous categories of classical software testing approaches have been proposed, whereas only a limited selection is currently available for quantum software. In this section, we highlight some techniques for testing quantum programs, which are described and categorized in Table 12.2.

  • Search-based testing: The search-based testing approach is not limited to evaluating classical software programs but is also increasingly being employed in quantum software [48]. The search-based method in testing quantum programs is a multifaceted approach that leverages optimization techniques, such as genetic algorithms (GAs) or random search [48], to automate the creation of test cases (test case generation), strategically arrange them in order of importance (test case prioritization), and reduce the test suite to its most efficient form (test suite minimization).

Table 12.2:Quantum software testing techniques, categories, and tools.

Techniques Categories Tools
Search-based testing White/black box and dynamic testing QuSBT [16]
MutTG [17]
Mutation testing White box and dynamic testing Muskit [24]
QMutPy [23, 41]
Property-based testing Black box and dynamic testing QSharpCheck [42]
Metamorphic testing Black box and dynamic testing MorphQ [43]
Fuzz testing Black box and dynamic testing QuanFuzz [20]
Combinatorial testing Black box and dynamic testing QuCAT [44, 45]
Multiple subroutines White/black box and dynamic/static testing QSharpTester [46]
Quantum symbolic execution White box and static testing symQV [47]
AST-based static analysis White box and static testing QChecker [27]

In the realm of search-based testing in QSE, Wang et al. [16] have proposed a tool called QuSBT, which employs GA to enhance testing effectiveness by maximizing the number of failing test cases in a test suite. QuSBT focuses on balancing the quality and cost of test inputs by using GA to find optimal test inputs that optimize quality. The authors validate QuSBT on IBM Qiskit framework. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of QuSBT in detecting failures in quantum programs. Similar to QuSBT, Wang et al. [17] introduce MutTG, which is also a search-based approach aimed at optimizing test generation for quantum programs. By creating a minimal test suite, MutTG aims to improve reliability by efficiently identifying and addressing program mutants.

  • Mutation testing: Mutation testing is another widely used software testing technique to assess the effectiveness of test cases by introducing artificial faults, known as “mutants,” into the code. It falls into the category of white box testing, wherein testers purposefully modify the source code to assess how well the software test suite can detect these alterations. The main objective of these modifications is to introduce defects into the software intentionally. Additionally, mutation testing serves as a popular approach for creating new tests involving small changes to a program that results in a new version of the software. In the realm of mutation testing, a substantial body of research has been developed, leading to notable contributions in the field. Collectively, these valuable insights and advancements collectively offer a comprehensive overview of the knowledge available on mutation testing and the tools used for this purpose.

  • One of these tools is Muskit [24], a mutation analysis tool designed for quantum programs coded in IBM’s Qiskit framework. It defines mutation operators on the gates of QPs and provides selection criteria to reduce the number of mutants generated. Muskit facilitates the execution of test cases on mutants and generates results for test analyses. It is accessible as a command line interface, GUI, and web application. Muskit comprises two primary components: Mutants Generator and Mutants Executor, in addition to Test Analyzer, which the users can implement as per their specific analysis requirements. The tool has been validated to generate and execute mutants for four QPs. Currently, Muskit cannot detect equivalent mutants, but the authors plan to implement techniques to detect them as more knowledge becomes available. Another notable tool, QMutPy [23, 41], is an extension of the open-source mutation testing tool MutPy [49], specifically designed for quantum programs. QMutPy tool introduces a novel set of mutation operators based on qubit measurements and quantum gates to generate mutants for testing quantum programs. QMutPy has been evaluated through a case study involving 24 real quantum programs written in IBM’s Qiskit library, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing test suite coverage and mutation score.

  • Property-based testing: Property-based testing, as a testing methodology, relies on the definition of essential properties to establish criteria and procedures for testing, with a particular focus on these properties [50]. In the context of QSE, Honarvar et al. [42] propose QSharpCheck, which is a property-based testing framework designed for Microsoft Q#. QSharpCheck is also equipped with five assertions, for example, “AssertProbability” and “AssertEntangled.” The authors evaluate the effectiveness of QSharpCheck via mutation analysis, and results show that QSharpCheck achieved 80% and 60% of mutation scores for two examples, respectively.

  • Metamorphic testing: Metamorphic testing [51, 43] refers to a software testing approach that focuses on creating test cases and validating test results by using metamorphic relationships, which specify the relationship between an output of a program and an input (which undergoes certain transformations). Abreu et al. [51] present metamorphic testing in oracle quantum programs. Their methodology relies on metamorphic relations, effectively resolving the well-known quantum measurement problem (i.e., wave function collapse). The authors validate their approach with IBM Qiskit, and the results show that, by using quantum search algorithms (such as Grover’s algorithm), their approach can speed up the testing process (improving the time complexity from O(N) to O(√N)). Another contribution of metamorphic testing is called MorphQ, proposed by Paltenghi and Pradel [43]. MorphQ consists of two components, that is, (1) a program generator that creates a diverse range of valid quantum programs and (2) a set of program transformations that leverage quantum-specific metamorphic relationships to alleviate the oracle problem. MorphQ is evaluated via Qiskit. In the experiments, it creates over 8,000 program pairs within 2 days, which exposes many crashes. Then, 13 bugs are found from those crashes.

  • Fuzz testing: Fuzz testing (also known as fuzzing) involves injecting unexpected inputs or random data (known as fuzz) into the software to assess its behaviors. In QSE, De las Cuevas et al. [52] propose QuanFuzz, which uses a matrix generator to generate test cases with higher coverage. QuanFuzz is validated over various quantum circuits to trigger sensitive branches for coverage testing. The testing results show that QuanFuzz achieves 20–60% more coverage compared to traditional testing input generation on quantum programs.

  • Combinatorial testing: Combinatorial testing is a testing technique in which multiple combinations of input parameters are used to perform testing [53]. Wang et al. [45] propose a combinatorial testing tool called QuCAT, which provides two functionalities for generating test suits. The first functionality generates a test suite of a given strength, and the second functionality generates test suites with increasing strength. The authors assess the efficiency and effectiveness of QuCAT via five quantum programs. Their results show that QuCAT with a low strength can find bugs efficiently, and QuCAT with a higher strength can perform better (finding more complicated bugs) with a higher cost.

  • Multiple subroutines: Multiple subroutine testing techniques focus on quantum programs with multisubroutines. For example, complex quantum programs can be divided into small subroutines, improving code reusability and maintainability. In 2022, Long and Zhao [46] propose QSharpTester, which is a tool for testing multi-subroutine quantum programs (in Q#). QSharpTester includes three test coverage criteria, that is, classical-superposition partition, classical-superposition-mixed partition, and entanglement partition for partitioning quantum programs. The authors use hundreds of mutation quantum programs derived from seven Q# programs to validate the effectiveness of QSharpTester. The experimental results show that QSharpTester performs well on a variety of quantum bugs in Q# on those mutation programs.

  • Quantum symbolic execution: Quantum symbolic execution proposed by Nan et al. [54] is a novel testing approach for generating high-coverage test cases to debug quantum programs. Quantum symbolic execution differs from classical symbolic execution by using quantum superposition and parallelism to store and continually divide the test case space into subsets based on conditional statements in the program, thereby enabling the identification of appropriate test cases for different code branches with reduced complexity. Moreover, the symbolic quantum programming [55] approach emphasizes the development of tools for symbolic manipulation of quantum circuits and testing quantum programs. It aims to support parallel and distributed computing and involves basic structures for local manipulation of qubits. Additionally, a new framework proposed by Bauer-Marquart et al. [47], symQV is a framework for writing and verifying quantum programs in the quantum circuit model, aiming for automated verification of quantum programs executed symbolically.

  • AST-based static analysis: As discussed in Quantum bugs section, QChecker [27] is a static analysis tool for detecting bugs of quantum programs developed in Qiskit. It encompasses modules that extract program data through ASTs and identify bugs by applying pattern-based detection methods. To the best of our knowledge, it is the only static analysis tool for testing and bug detection in quantum software.

12.3.1 Noise in quantum computing

Quantum noise presents a formidable challenge within the domain of quantum computing, posing a significant obstacle to achieving the desired levels of computational accuracy. In contrast to CCs, where outcomes are deterministically predictable, quantum programs are susceptible to the disruptive effects of quantum noise, resulting in unanticipated errors and deviations from anticipated results [56]. Thus, understanding and modeling quantum noise is crucial for software developers transitioning from classical programming to quantum programming.

Pan et al. [57] worked on the first study to explore quantum noise from a SE perspective. In another work, Resch and Karpuzcu [58] attempted to present various causes of quantum noise. In addition, Martina et al. [59] identified machine learning to detect computer noise in the hardware of noisy intermediate scale QCs because each computer has a noise footprint that can be learned about. However, a new approach presented by Muqeet et al. [60] can reduce noise’s effect on the test results of a quantum program called QOIN.

12.4 Quantum software debugging

Debugging, an essential part of software development, takes a whole new dimension in the quantum realm. QCs operate on the principles of quantum physics, a field known for its counterintuitive and amusing properties. Particles exist in superposition in this quantum universe, capable of representing many values at the same time. In the quantum world, measurement, which is a crucial debugging step in classical computing, takes on a dual purpose. While in superposition, quantum bits exist in an indeterminate state. However, when measured, this quantum superposition collapses, potentially resulting in unintentional errors and rendering typical debugging approaches ineffective.

Debugging quantum software confronts the Heisenberg uncertainty principle [61], which underscores the challenges of quantum measurement. In classical computing, measurements reveal the state of a variable without altering it. In quantum computing, measurement disrupts the state of a qubit, introducing quantum uncertainty into the debugging process. Understanding how measurements affect the quantum state is essential for effective debugging [62].

12.4.1 Debugging tactics in classical SE

Miranskyy et al. [40] categorize debugging tactics into three groups, that is, (1) backtracking, (2) cause elimination, and (3) brute force, each with its strengths and challenges. These three tactics apply in both the classical and quantum SE:

  • Backtracking tactics: Backtracking tactics use conventional debugging techniques to trace quantum bugs systematically [40]. Using the quantum stack trace, developers may trace bugs back to their origin, providing significant insights into the quantum error propagation mechanism. This method helps in locating the specific line of code containing the incorrect code, which speeds up the debugging process. It should be emphasized, however, that quantum stack traces can be lengthy, especially in complex quantum algorithms, and that prolonged retracing may be resource-intensive, potentially slowing down debugging procedures.

  • Cause elimination tactics: Cause elimination tactics provide an effective strategy for resolving bugs in quantum software. This approach involves systematically ruling out potential causes of bugs in quantum programs, gradually narrowing down to the root cause [40]. Developers can make this tactic a valuable debugging strategy when they use repetitive cause elimination tactics. For this reason, this tactic would be time-consuming due to the nature of the process. On the other hand, this approach is remarkably efficacious when dealing with complex bugs. Depending on the complexity of the program, cause elimination strategies may be resource-intensive as well.

  • Brute force tactics: This methodology comprises thorough testing and analysis of quantum states in order to detect anomalies and bugs. Developers can find errors that may not be seen using conventional debugging methods by carefully investigating the whole range of parameters and quantum state shifts, providing excellent precision in spotting bugs [40]. However, it is essential to note that brute force approaches are resource-intensive, costing a significant amount of processing power and time. The computational cost associated with brute force debugging in large-scale quantum systems may make it impracticable.

12.4.2 Debugging tactics in QSE

Several debugging techniques have been proposed and applied in QSE. The most popular technique is to utilize assertions in debugging. Some quantum platforms, like IBM quantum platform [63], also provide interactive debugging services. We will discuss these techniques in detail below.

12.4.2.1 Assertion-based debugging

Assertion-based debugging is a methodology where developers embed specific statements, or assertions, within the quantum code to define expected behaviors and outcomes. These assertions act as checkpoints, serving as benchmarks for the quantum program’s execution. During debugging, the system automatically verifies whether these assertions hold true. If an assertion fails, it signals a deviation from the expected behavior, highlighting potential errors or bugs in the code. This approach enhances the developer’s ability to systematically and proactively validate the correctness of quantum programs, allowing for early detection and resolution of issues before they become more complex or problematic.

There are three essential types of quantum assertions within the realm of quantum computing. First, classical assertions are utilized to confirm the proper interaction of classical components in hybrid quantum-classical systems with quantum processes. Second, superposition assertions employ propositional logic implication to assess the presence of a uniform quantum superposition state. Last but not least, entanglement assertions serve a vital role in detecting errors in quantum circuits by ensuring the persistence of specific entangled states, a crucial task due to the fragile nature of quantum systems. Together, these assertion types collectively contribute to the verification and maintenance of desired quantum behaviors and states in quantum programs.

Recent advancements in quantum computing validation, particularly the introduction of quantum assertions, represent a significant stride in the field. Quantum assertions play a pivotal role in verifying the functionality of quantum programs and addressing the intricate challenges associated with their development. Li et al. [30] state that quantum assertions act as a vital tool for debugging quantum programs and mitigating hardware errors, addressing the unique challenges presented by quantum properties like the no-cloning theorem and potentially destructive measurements. Through projection-based monitoring and statistical assertion techniques, quantum assertions offer a promising avenue not only for debugging but also for error mitigation and lightweight error correction. In essence, quantum assertions offer a compelling solution to improve the dependability of quantum computing systems, marking a substantial step forward in the quantum computing landscape.

The work by Huang and Martonosi [28] outlines a comprehensive strategy for deploying and verifying quantum program assertions through statistical testing. It addresses diverse bug types and defense types critical for improving the reliability and correctness of quantum programs. It also introduces contingency table analysis as a powerful tool for validating intermediate states, especially in quantum chemistry simulations. The experiment extends across multiple case studies. In the context of quantum chemistry simulations, precise classical input parameters and qubit initial values are paramount, and precondition assertions serve to validate these inputs. Postcondition assertions focus on preserving symmetry in quantum models. Furthermore, Grover’s search algorithm [64] demonstrates how higher-level quantum development platforms, like ProjectQ [65], simplify the placement of assertions, particularly in the context of controlled operations. Shor’s algorithm [66] emphasizes the importance of product state assertions to validate the correct deallocation of ancillary qubits in quantum subroutines. These findings underscore the need for structured debugging methodologies, including assertion checks, in quantum program development.

In a series of experiments conducted on a 20-qubit IBMQ QC, Liu et al. [31] explore the impact of dynamic runtime assertions in quantum computing. The study investigates various types of assertions and integrates them into different quantum algorithms like quantum Fourier transform [67], quantum phase estimation [68], Bernstein Vaziani [69], and more. The study also introduces the concept of asserting deallocated ancillary qubits to maintain program correctness. The results indicate a marked improvement in quantum algorithm precision when executed on real quantum hardware. The open-source Qiskit framework incorporates these assertion circuits for broader quantum computing community access.

The work by Li et al. [29] introduces Proq, a projection-based runtime assertion scheme that uses projection operators as predicates in assert primitives. Proq claims to enhance expressive power and reduce assertion overhead compared to existing quantum assertion schemes. The study encompasses theoretical foundations and practical transformations to make projection-based assertions feasible on measurement-restricted QCs. Although Proq is promising, the work lacks empirical validation of the Proq scheme through practical demonstrations or experiments on real-world quantum programs. Also, the complexity introduced by using projection operators may pose a challenge, especially for quantum developers without a deep understanding of quantum mechanics.

Metwalli and Van Meter [70] propose the Quantum Circuit Slicing tool, drawing inspiration from manual slicing and breakpoints. Quantum Circuit Slicing tool simplifies complex quantum circuits by dividing them into manageable slices for in-depth examination and debugging. A beta version of the tool was released for testing to a group of developers, who found it invaluable for simplifying circuits, enhancing their understanding, and locating bugs through the gate tracking feature. While the results are promising, the work could benefit from more detailed explanations of experiments and findings.

Witharana et al. [71] present an automated approach for generating quantum assertions to validate quantum circuits. The performing of quAssert involves two stages, that is, mining assertions and inserting assertions. In the first stage, quAssert can automatically uncover special properties of a quantum circuit, such as superposition, and entangled states, using statistical methods. These uncovered properties indicate the locations for inserting assertions. Then, in stage 2, quAssert will place quantum assertions automatically and maximize coverage. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of quAssert using a suite of quantum benchmarks including Shor’s algorithm and Grover’s algorithm. The results show that automatically inserted assertions can expose bugs efficiently, for example, it can quickly detect a quantum bug with 15 assertions.

12.4.2.2 Interactive debugging

Interactive debugging is a real-time debugging technique that helps developers identify and rectify bugs as they run the program. The instantaneous insights of bugs provided in interactive debugging make it a rapid and time-efficient debugging strategy. However, it may not be suitable for quantum programs because of the well-known quantum measurement problem (i.e., wave function collapse).

The composer from IBM quantum platform [63] provides an interactive debugging environment, enhancing the debugging process for quantum circuits. Particularly, the platform offers an “inspect” functionality within the composer, enabling a thorough inspection of the circuit gate-by-gate or layer-by-layer.

In Figure 12.1, there is an example that indicates using the “inspect” feature to debug a two-qubit quantum circuit. As you can see from the figure, this feature allows users to observe the functioning of the circuit through each gate or layer by clicking the “next” button in the composer.

As the debugger, “inspect” steps through the gates or layers of the quantum circuit, users can analyze the changes in the outcome probability for every computational quantum state, as depicted in Figure 12.2. As you can see from the figure, during the process of “inspect,” developers can check the probabilities of the quantum states instantly.

Furthermore, Figure 12.3 illustrates the Q-Sphere representation, another valuable tool for visualizing the quantum states during the debugging process. The Q-Sphere provides a comprehensive view of the quantum state, allowing users to gain insights into the state’s evolution and potential issues.

12.4.2.3 Debugging in local IDEs

Debugging tools are available in integrated development environments (IDEs), such as PyCharm (for Python programming, JetBrains [72]). The demonstration of Figure 12.4 involves importing Qiskit, creating a simple quantum code, and intentionally inducing errors to test the debugging features. Two key characteristics of the debugging process are highlighted.

In Figure 12.4, breakpoints are utilized for interactive debugging. Breakpoints act as temporary stops in the code, instructing the debugger to pause before executing the subsequent line. This facilitates a detailed analysis of the code at the designated breakpoint, aiding in effective debugging. The red circle in the code’s left sidebar signifies the introduced breakpoint.

Upon activation of the debugger, Figure 12.5 demonstrates how the debugger displays detailed information about variables up to the breakpoint. This information is presented in the lower area of the window, enabling users to evaluate variables and understand the code’s state at the breakpoint.

The second feature involves “code inspections,” as illustrated in Figure 12.6. This functionality provides debugging tips whenever an error is identified. When the mouse hovers over the line containing the error, a pop-up reveals information about the type of error and offers debugging recommendations. In this context, a bug related to incorrect arguments for the circuit gate is discovered, and the debugging actions are provided for resolution.

To summarize, debugging techniques (e.g., assertion-based debugging and interactive debugging) have been developed in QSE. However, due to the nature of quantum mechanics, both the literature and the industry require more novel proposals and tools to debug quantum programs more efficiently and effectively (just like the tools that developers are using in classical SE).

12.5 Challenges and opportunities

Both research challenges and opportunities exist in the field of QSE. In this section, we will highlight some of the key challenges and opportunities.

12.5.1 QSE research challenges

We present three major challenges in testing and debugging quantum software as follows:

  • First, the literature in QSE lacks automation for fixing quantum software bugs. Bug pattern detection is a common static approach to analyze bugs. It helps developers understand common bug categories and characteristics. Later on, those characteristics can be used to develop tools that can scan source code to find bugs. In classical SE, previous studies show that bug pattern analysis and detection can help in developing automated techniques to detect bugs from existing source code more effectively and efficiently [73]. However, the research on bug patterns in QSE is still immature. Previous studies of bug patterns (such as Bugs4Q by Zhao et al. [35]) and bug-fix patterns (e.g., Q-Diff [37]) need to be extended to the next step. For example, the characteristics of bugs can be used as inputs for classification or clustering models (e.g., support vector machine and K-means) to detect bug patterns.

  • Our initial step in bug-fix pattern detection [37] can be used to predict fix patterns for existing quantum software bugs. Another challenge for QSE is the lack of data. This leads to the fact that the datasets for training machine learning models in QSE are small. We can use simple machine learning models (decision trees and support vector machine), cross-validation, and semi-supervised learning approaches for limited data.

  • Second, it is challenging to test quantum software because of its indeterminacy. As mentioned in Quantum software testing section, indeterminacy is the nature of quantum computing. However, indeterminacy brings significant challenges to testing and debugging quantum programs. For example, quantum programs produce probabilistic results because of randomness. Such cases can cause flaky tests, which means that the same test case can fail in some cases and pass in other cases. In reality, enterprises suffer from flaky tests, for example, 4.5% of test cases fail because of flaky tests in Google [12].

  • Last but not least, interactive debugging in quantum computing poses unique challenges. Quantum programs operate in superposition, making observation complex due to state collapse risks. Entanglement adds complexity as debugging requires managing correlated qubits. Limited classical information, probabilistic outcomes, and complex gate sequences further complicate debugging. Developing effective debugging tools tailored to quantum systems is challenging. Scalability concerns arise with larger quantum systems, and real-time interaction introduces issues like latency and responsiveness. Specialized debugging tools and methodologies are essential for ensuring the reliability and correctness of quantum software.

12.5.2 Future research directions in QSE

We highlight three research opportunities/directions with challenges for researchers:

  • First, leverage classical SE best practices, especially those techniques that have been proven to be effective in dynamic programming and machine learning because of their random nature. Classical SE has developed for multiple decades. Methods and tools are widely studied in all areas of SE such as requirements engineering, system modeling, compliance, secure engineering, verification, validation, maintenance, and evolution. Since QSE is still immature, one can leverage classical SE best practices on QSE. More specifically, the indeterminacy of quantum computing is similar to dynamic or stochastic programming. Thus, testing techniques (e.g., search-based software testing [21]) that are proven to be effective in these domains can be potentially applied to QSE.

  • Second, incorporate bug-fix pattern detection into debugging to predict fix patterns for existing bugs. Due to the short history of QSE and quantum software development, existing research on QSE is mainly on bug pattern analysis [11]. However, in classical SE, bug pattern analysis is usually the initial step for automated fixing. A typical research agenda for automated fixing is (1) bug pattern analysis, (2) bug pattern classification, (3) bug-fix pattern analysis, and (4) fix prediction for existing bugs. Our previous study on bug-fix pattern recognition is the first research on Step 3. The next step is to utilize classical clustering or classification algorithms (such as SVM [74] and K-means [75]) and artificial neural networks (such as LSTM [76] and GRU [77]) to predict a fix pattern for an existing bug in quantum software.

  • Last but not list, combine artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing. In the dynamic landscape of computer science, quantum computing, and AI stand as groundbreaking milestones. Quantum computing, with its unparalleled computational capabilities, is redefining the boundaries of what is computationally feasible. Concurrently, the advent of neurosymbolic AI, integration of symbolic and neural techniques,1

    12.6 Conclusions

    QSE is a “child” community in SE, and it has a relatively short history compared to the history of its “parent.” However, because of the potential of quantum computing and recent breakthroughs in quantum hardware, the research and development of quantum software are rapidly evolving. More and more researchers and practitioners joined the community, and they started bringing SE best practices into the world of quantum computing. On October 30, 2023, President Biden directed the most sweeping actions to protect Americans from the potential risks of AI systems. These actions include but are not limited to developing standards, tools, and tests to help ensure that AI systems are safe, secure, and trustworthy [78]. As the power of QCs is combined with AI models (e.g., quantum neural networks proposed by Altaisky [79]), it is more urgent than ever to harness quantum AI software through standards and testing against classical and quantum threats.

    In this chapter, we conduct a survey of testing and debugging methods and tools for quantum software. We analyze bug patterns, bug pattern detections, testing tactics, and debugging tactics. We also highlight some common and popular techniques in quantum software testing and debugging. We discuss the challenges and opportunities for the research field of QC software. The ultimate goal is to automate the process of testing and debugging quantum software to speed up development and improve its quality. We believe that this work would be of interest to practitioners creating quantum programs as well as researchers developing the next generations of tooling for QC.

13 Quantum-enhanced neural networks: bridging the quantum algorithm and machine learning

Manisa Manoswini
Debasish Swapnesh Kumar Nayak
Tejaswini Das
Tripti Swarnkar

Abstract

Using quantum concepts like superposition and entanglement, quantum-enhanced neural networks (QENN) combine machine learning (ML) and quantum computing to improve neural network performance. They are expected to have a revolutionary influence on optimization, pattern recognition, and complex data analysis. In this work, authors discuss the principles of quantum computing, including superposition, entanglement, and quantum gates, before introducing many quantum ML (QML) techniques, including Grover’s search, Shor’s factoring, and quantum annealing. Following that, it discusses the fundamentals of neural networks for problems like image recognition and natural language processing while addressing issues with big data and high-dimensional features. This work focuses on using quantum processors to speed up traditional ML tasks by combining quantum algorithms with neural networks to generate hybrid models. It investigates quantum kernel techniques, quantum variational algorithms, and QENN, demonstrating their potential to improve conventional neural network frameworks. In addition to this authors also include real-world applications in fields including drug development, materials research, finance, and optimization to show the revolutionary effects of quantum-enhanced machine learning (QEML) on current problems. In conclusion, this chapter provides a thorough review of QML, highlighting the synergy between quantum algorithms and neural networks. It offers unique insights into the field’s current state, practical applications, and hopes for defining the future of artificial intelligence through quantum computational paradigms.

Keywords: Quantum computing, quantum-enhanced neural networks, machine learning, convolutional neural network, high-dimension features,

13.1 Introduction

The development of quantum machine learning (QML) is evidence of human curiosity and the never-ending quest for new ideas. Quantum physics altered our knowledge of the fundamental components of the cosmos around the turn of the twentieth century. By frequently pushing the limits of classical physics, pioneers like Max Planck, Albert Einstein, and Niels Bohr established the foundation for what would eventually become quantum computing [1, 2, 3].

A unique abstraction has developed in the dynamic world of technology and artificial intelligence, and it has the potential to revolutionize how authors will approach optimization, pattern recognition, and complex data analysis. Quantum-enhanced neural network (QENN) is a revolutionary paradigm that combines the strength of quantum computing with the intelligence of neural networks to open up a range of possibilities that were previously only possible in science fiction. This abstraction has the potential to transform machine learning (ML) and push the boundaries of what authors thought was possible by utilizing the special principles of quantum physics [4].

The development of QML is evidence of human curiosity and the never-ending quest for new ideas. Quantum physics altered our knowledge of the fundamental components of the cosmos around the turn of the twentieth century. By frequently pushing the limits of classical physics, pioneers like Max Planck, Albert Einstein, and Niels Bohr established the foundation for what would eventually become quantum computing.

The concept of quantum computing began to take shape in the second phase of the twentieth centennial. The groundbreaking concept of Richard Feynman, which involved simulating quantum phenomena using quantum systems, captured the attention of scientists and computer engineers. Quantum algorithms, the brilliant creations of luminaries like David Deutsch, Lov Grover, and Peter Shor, began to take shape in the following decades. These algorithms provide unheard-of speeds for resolving issues that were intractable by conventional computers [5].

Successful advancement has been made in the domain of computational intelligence, notably in the domain of ML, in recent years [6, 7]. The potential of learning machines is amply illustrated by a recent accomplishment that was previously believed to be decades away – a computer beating a skilled human player at Go [8]. The foundations of a brand-new field termed QML are being laid in parallel with this. The field of artificial intelligence could be completely transformed by it, just as quantum information processing has done for its conventional counterpart [9]. The emergence of neural networks and ML heralded a new age in artificial intelligence, coinciding with advances in quantum computing. It became clearer that neural networks were capable of tackling challenging tasks, for example, NLP and picture identification. Four key players are involved with the introduction of NISQ (noisy intermediate-scale quantum) technology as shown in Figure 13.1.

The real work of creating qubits and the associated hardware is handled by engineers and physicists, while mathematicians, computer scientists, and theorists in general are occupied with expanding the boundaries of quantum information and quantum algorithms.

Quantum computing might deliver benefits in the sectors of ML and neural networks. With a slew of game-changing advantages, quantum computing holds immense potential in the domains of ML and neural networks. Fundamentally, the capacity for achieving exponential speedup in particular computations stands out as a game-changer, with quantum algorithms like Grover’s search and Shor’s factoring poised to outperform their classical counterparts and potentially speeding up ML tasks like data search and factorization. The parallelism provided by superposition, in which quantum bits can concurrently exist in multiple states, further boosts its prowess. This remarkable ability of quantum computers to explore numerous problem solutions concurrently is beneficial for optimization and pattern recognition tasks in ML. It is also the phenomenon targeted by specialized QML algorithms.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAQA) is one example of a quantum variational algorithm that brings improved efficiency to solving optimization issues and promises performance improvements across various ML tasks. The consequences of quantum computing for encryption, driven by decomposition and search capabilities, demonstrate the need for cryptography after quantum computing for ML protection of systems at identical times. Quantum computers also focus on energy economy and offer resource frugality for certain activities, which is advantageous for ML applications on devices with limited resources. In conclusion, the incorporation of quantum-enhanced techniques into ML and neural networks offers some degree of future-proofing as quantum computing develops, positioning itself strategically to adapt to developing quantum technologies, and leaving an enduring imprint on the future of artificial intelligence.

13.1.1 Motive and background

This chapter sets out on a journey through the complex world of quantum computing, concentrating on the fundamental ideas behind this groundbreaking discipline. Its core ideas – superposition, entanglement, and quantum gates – serve as the cornerstone for the subsequent quantum algorithms. These techniques, such as Grover’s search, Shor’s factoring, and quantum annealing, have the potential to completely alter the ML environment by providing unheard-of computational benefits.

Additionally, the core of this chapter is grounded in tackling the enormous difficulties and complexity faced by conventional neural networks in the fluid environment of modern artificial intelligence. Quantum computing appears as a powerful ally at a time characterized by an enormous influx of data and the deep complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces. Its ability to simultaneously analyze enormous amounts of data opens the door to speeding up typical ML tasks and ushers in a new era in which quantum and classical computing combine to achieve previously unimaginable results [10].

Our main concern in this part is developing hybrid models that seamlessly combine the fields of quantum computing and neural networks. These novel models, such as quantum kernel methods, quantum variational algorithms, and quantum-enhanced neural networks, are closely examined. They present the intriguing possibility of utilizing the special advantages of quantum computing to not only accelerate but also dramatically improve conventional neural network frameworks.

This chapter leaves the theoretical sphere and enters the domain of application by investigating concrete real-world uses of QEML. These applications cover important areas like medication discovery, materials science, financial modeling, and problems with optimization. Here, researchers see the practical and revolutionary potential of QEML in solving current real-world issues and grasping fresh chances for innovation.

Finally, the purpose of this chapter is to go into the frontier of QML and demonstrate the complicated relationship between quantum algorithms and neural networks. It provides clear insights into the current status of the science, relevant applications, and a vision for molding artificial intelligence via the prism of quantum computing paradigms. This journey takes place against a backdrop of infinite possibilities, where the interwoven worlds of quantum theory and ML define the cutting-edge of modern science, promising revolutionary advances in the area.

13.2 Quantum principles

Quantum computing examines information processing utilizing quantum mechanical systems. Quantum computers use qubits, which can simultaneously represent the combination of 0 and 1, enabling exponentially more computing possibilities than traditional computers that handle individual bits. Qubits are capable of carrying out complicated calculations that are beyond the scope of conventional computers because of quantum features like superposition and entanglement. Even the most sophisticated supercomputers may not be able to tackle the computational issues that this prospective platform could tackle. The foundations of quantum computing, alternative qubit representations, and how quantum features are used for computation are all covered in this section.

13.2.1 Superposition

A basic notion in quantum computing is superposition, which allows quantum particles, or qubits, to be present at the same time in different states. Keeping things simple, the idea of a qubit will be taught using the illustration of a photon in this section. This example shows that one bit of data is encoded by the polarization of a photon, which is related to its geometric direction. Specifically, a photon that is horizontally polarized represents a traditional bit 0, while a photon that is vertically polarized represents a traditional bit 1 [11].

In Figure 13.1, photons are generated and then flow through a section known as Filter-V, which only allows photons that are vertically polarized to pass through. To simplify the scenario, authors suppose that a single photon enters the setup at a time. The next part, the polarization beam splitter (PBS), works like this: For vertically polarized photons, the detector marked DV is used for transmission, while for horizontally polarized photons, the detector named DH is used for redirection and measurement. Consequently, all incoming photons in this setup (Figure 13.2) will exhibit their vertical polarization when measured at DV.

On the other hand, according to Figure 13.3, if “Filter-45” is placed in between Filter-V and PBS, each detector has a 12% probability of detecting a horizontally or vertically divided photon.

The probability amplitudes for each should be 1/2, since the chance of finding either vertically or horizontally polarized photons at the PBS is 1/2. As a result, the photon’s condition just before PBS can be shown as

(13.1)$|\psi› = 1/\sqrt{}2\ |H› + 1\ /\sqrt{}2\ |V›$

Since the bit “1” in expression (13.1) is represented by |V) and the bit “0” by |H), respectively, the expression is expressed as

(13.2)$|\psi› = 1/\sqrt{}2\ |0›) + 1\ /\sqrt{}2\ |1›$

In this state of preparation, a photon’s digital information is either “0” or “1.” It is possible to interpret eq. (13.2) as indicating that the states “0” and “1” are both present simultaneously. This unique circumstance is known as a superposition condition.

In the superposition state (5), two qubits are shown as follows:

13.3 Entanglement: a fascinating phenomenon of quantum physics

One of the most useful tools in quantum computing is entanglement. Qubits can share information and carry out intricate operations in ways that regular bits cannot when they are entangled. This characteristic is crucial for developing quantum algorithms, which can solve some problems significantly more quickly than conventional algorithms [12]. In the 1970s, computer reversibility emerged as a prominent area of discussion. One key concept in computing is reversible computing, which lets you go back from an output state to the input state. This idea consists of two separate components:

13.4 Physical reversibility

Physical reversibility indicates the fact that once an input is removed, the data is irreversibly lost. Logical reversibility, on the other hand, emphasizes the capacity to reform the data from the outcome. The NAND gate is unalterable because it is impossible to recreate the inputs from the outcome data. The NAND gate has a single output and two inputs. The NOT gate, on the other hand, is reversible [13].

Because its input and output are mapped one-to-one, reversible logic guarantees that no data is lost and no energy is wasted. Quantum gates are a significant advantage of quantum computing due to their reversibility. With quantum computers, it is possible to avoid the irreversibility that accompanies classical processing and avoid information loss. Quantum gates are the building components of quantum circuits in the computation model known as quantum circuits [14]. Qubits are subjected to typical gates and operations. The single-qubit quantum gates that include H, X, Y, Z, T, and I, as well as the Phase gate, are basic and significant. Swap, CZ, and CNOT gates are two-qubit quantum gates; Toffoli and Fredkin gates are three-qubit quantum gates. Single-qubit and two-qubit quantum gates are utilized by traditional logic gates like NAND, AND, NOR, XOR, and OR. A gate with n qubits is represented as a 2n × 2n matrix. In contrast, 4 × 4 matrices represent two-qubit gates, and single-qubit gates are represented as 2 × 2 matrices.

|0› → A|0› + B|1›
|1› → C|0› + D|1›

The aforementioned operation can be› expressed in a matrix as follows:

$\begin{matrix} {A\ C} \\ {B\ D} \\ \ \\ \end{matrix}$

13.4.1 Interaction and measure of qubits

The interaction with qubits is in the context of different quantum computer physical realizations like neutral atoms and spin qubits. It details the manipulation and measurement of qubits in these systems as follows:

  • Neutral atom realization: This method represents qubits by using the electron quantum states of neutral atoms. An electron can be in one of two states: excited (mapped to |1) or ground (mapped to |0). An electron can move between these states by exposing the atom to a specified energy level for a set amount of time. The electron may also be put in a superposition state, where it is simultaneously in |0 and |1 by altering the illumination time.

  • Realization of spin qubits: Spin qubits are yet another physical embodiment of qubits. A powerful magnetic field is used to initialize them in a particular state, usually all spin-up (representing the 0 state), at the start. Electromagnetic pulses are used to individually control each of these qubits. The applied electromagnetic pulse’s amplitude and length determine the qubit’s state.

Due to the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics, continuous measurement at every place is not possible in quantum computing. Because there is inherent uncertainty in every measurement, it is impossible to take continuous measurements. It is essential to have a physical apparatus that can precisely measure all of the qubit states involved in the computation in order to obtain the outcome of quantum computations.

Preparing quantum systems for computations, ensuring they remain in a coherent state, and carrying out measurements that produce useful data from the quantum states are the key hurdles in quantum computing. This is crucial for understanding and applying the quantum data produced by the computation. To fully utilize the capabilities of quantum computing technology, these obstacles must be overcome.

13.5 Techniques for QML

ML is based on teaching computers to learn via data processing and analysis processes. This field combines artificial intelligence with computational statistics at the intersection of computer science and statistics. A subset of classical ML called deep learning (both supervised and unsupervised) has proven to be very helpful for tasks like speech recognition, image classification, pattern detection, and managing large datasets. It has consequently attracted a lot of interest and funding from numerous companies.

However, there is an increasing demand for fresh strategies to automatically manage, organize, and categorize the vast amounts of data authors encounter every day. Traditional ML is adaptive and agile and excels at seeing patterns, but it may not be able to address some complicated problems effectively.

Businesses that handle large database administration are aware of these drawbacks and are eager to explore other methods. One approach is to use QML. In order to potentially facilitate more efficient problem-solving, QML aims to integrate ML algorithms within quantum systems. It achieves this by utilizing entanglement and superposition, two examples of quantum properties.

Quantum computers exploit superposition states to allow for the simultaneous execution of several tasks. This provides a definite speed and data processing advantage over standard ML methods. QML uses quantum algorithms to perform classical algorithm-intensive tasks on a quantum computer. This enables both unsupervised and supervised algorithms to be used to classify, categorize, and analyze data. Models such as support vector machines or quantum neural networks are frequently used to implement these strategies. As an outcome, QML has the capability to totally revolutionize how authors handle and evaluate data, opening up new opportunities for application development [16]. A brief explanation of each of the listed quantum machines learning techniques may be found in the following section.

13.5.1 Grover’s search: quantum space search revolutionized

Grover’s algorithm is an unstructured search quantum algorithm that uses only O(N) function evaluations, where N is the size of the function’s domain, to identify the unique data to a black box operation that yields a given output value. Lov Grover invented it in 1996 [17]. Because one must often explore half the domain to discover the proper input, Umesh Vazirani, Gilles Brassard, Ethan Bernstein, and Charles H. Bennett demonstrated that the function (N) must be evaluated there to be a quantum solution to the issue.

Grover’s technique, according to Ethan Bernstein, Gilles Brassard, Charles H. Bennett and Umesh Vazirani, is asymptotically optimum since evaluating the function (N) times is required for any quantum solution of the issue [18]. Grover’s approach to unstructured search only provides a quadratic speedup over solution; this implies that Grover’s algorithm will not solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time, because the square root of an exponential function is an exponential function rather than a polynomial function [9]. Grover’s approach only provides a quadratic speedup over other quantum algorithms, which may provide an exponential speedup over their conventional counterparts. Grover’s approach may accelerate a wide range of tasks, and even quadratic acceleration becomes noticeable when N is big.

Grover’s approach can brute-force a 256-bit key in 2,128 iterations and a 128-bit key in around 264 iterations. However, Grover’s technique may not represent a considerably bigger danger to encryption than commonly utilized classical methods [19].

13.5.2 Application and drawbacks

Many calculations can be accelerated using Grover’s approach, and modifications like amplitude amplification [20, 21, 22], specifically an exhaustive search subroutine, are usually included in algorithms for NP-complete problems, and Grover’s method helps to speed this up [15]. Among them is the greatest 3SAT approach available right now. In [23], the input does not need to be provided in the form of an oracle for these techniques because Grover’s method is used with an explicit function, like verifying if a collection of bits fulfills a 3SAT instance.

13.5.3 Cryptography

Grover’s approach is used to address the function inversion problem. For instance, function like y = f(x), which can be evaluated on a quantum computer, can use Grover’s approach to compute x given y. Grover’s approach significantly accelerates a variety of encryption techniques, including collision and preimage attacks [24]. Because the parallel rho algorithm, for example, may discover a collision in SHA2 quicker than Grover’s technique, this may not be the most effective option [25].

  • Drawbacks: The technique was initially described as a database search algorithm in Grover’s article, and this usage persists to this day. In this analogy, the database is a table that is indexed by the pertinent input and contains every output produced by the function. However, there is no explicit display of this database. Rather, an oracle is contacted to evaluate a piece of information based on its index. The time it takes to go through an entire storage item by item and convert it to this specification may outrun Grover’s search. Grover’s technique might be viewed of as satisfying a constraint or solving an equation to account for such consequences. In these cases, the oracle is not used in the search process; rather, it is used to validate the constraint.

Traditional search algorithms frequently rely on such optimizations to avoid exhaustive searches, but this separation typically prevents algorithmic optimizations [26]. Grover’s oracle is simple to construct and can solve a wide range of constraint fulfillment and optimization issues [27].

The fundamental impediment to the adoption of Grover’s technique is that the resulting quadratic speedup is insufficient to compensate for the considerable cost of short-term quantum computing [28]. These data speedups may be attainable in subsequent generations of fault-tolerant quantum machines with improved hardware performance.
